Government administration.

Lawyers.

Truck drivers.

Shipping captains.

Manufacturing workers.

Coders.

Pretty much anything that doesn't require a ton of individualized creativity...

Fast food ordering is the immediate obvious one. The terminals are already designed for use with an absolute minimum of training, and for those that are scared of buttons, voice recognition software is getting scary-good (see Android phones and google voice search). Hell, a lot of people would probably prefer to just walk up and punch in their own order rather than dealing with the common minimum-wage recipient who doesn't actually want to be there and certainly could care less about you or your order. Some places will cater to those who want to interact with a human, and the people who want that will be willing to pay the premium for it.

The bigger concern I have is how we handle the portion of the population that does become jobless because of automation. So long as our culture insists that a person's only value is their labor but that you must pay up front for education, those people have no place. So, what do they do? Become homeless? Can we handle having 5-10% of our population on the streets? Do we go more socialist and ensure that everyone has the basic necessities of life (food, water, shelter)? I don't have an answer, but I see it being the big problem we'll have to address if we want to advance to the Star Trekkian utopia of having replicators and working for personal enrichment instead of survival.

  • Accountants. There are companies already working on eliminating accountants almost entirely.

  • Call centre employees. There are computer programs that use voice recordings to answer most questions. These already exist and will become better and more common over the next 5 years.

  • Drivers of all sorts. There are loads of mining vehicles that are automated already. Trains have been automated for years in Australia with union required drivers sitting onboard "in case something goes wrong".

  • Journalists. Already the simple reporting (sports writeups, economic news) is done by machines, it shouldn't be long until almost all of it is.

I think 95% of the jobs in these sectors will be lost in the next 15 years with only a few remaining for the odd cases that machines aren't flexible enough to handle.
